claims.quote: Arulkumaran et al. offer an accessible entry point by situating deep RL as a transformative development within artificial intelligence, arguing that deep learning is enabling reinforcement learning to scale to previously intractable problems, such as learning control policies directly from raw pixel inputs [arxiv_1708.05866].

Li produces two extensive overview treatments that share a common organizational framework built around six core elements, six important mechanisms, and twelve applications [arxiv_1701.07274; arxiv_1810.06339].

Mousavi et al. survey the intersection of deep learning and reinforcement learning, highlighting how deep representations have enabled agents to learn useful features for decision-making [arxiv_1806.08894].

The extension of deep RL to multiagent environments introduces substantial additional complexity, as the future rewards of any agent depend on the joint actions of all participants [arxiv_2106.15691].
Agent modeling [arxiv_1907.09597] and communication mechanisms such as message-dropout [arxiv_1902.06527] represent complementary strategies for improving coordination in multiagent systems.

A dominant design paradigm in cooperative settings is centralized training with decentralized execution (CTDE), which permits agents to share global information during training while acting on local observations at deployment.

Training agents from scratch in each new environment remains computationally prohibitive [arxiv_1811.12560; arxiv_1708.05866], and transfer learning offers a principled solution by leveraging knowledge acquired in source tasks to accelerate learning in related target tasks [ss_475943; arxiv_2009.07888].
Policy distillation constitutes a further mechanism for knowledge transfer, compressing larger teacher networks into smaller student networks while preserving performance.

Undirected approaches, such as ε-greedy policies or Gaussian noise injection, are widely used in practice [arxiv_1812.05551], yet they are known to fail in off-policy continuous control settings [arxiv_2210.00293].

Bayesian and distributional approaches offer a more principled resolution to the exploration–exploitation dilemma. Tang and Agrawal [arxiv_1805.01907] propose a distributional RL framework that conceptually unifies several prior exploration methods, while Osband et al. [arxiv_1703.07608] demonstrate that randomized value functions can guide deep exploration in a statistically efficient manner.

Mnih et al. [arxiv_1602.01783] propose asynchronous gradient descent as a lightweight yet effective training framework, demonstrating that parallel actor-learners exert a stabilizing effect on training across multiple standard RL algorithms.

Miao et al. [arxiv_2106.02229] demonstrate that differentiable architecture search techniques, specifically adaptations of DARTS, can be applied to RL and yield architectures achieving up to 250% of the performance of manually designed counterparts across both discrete and continuous action spaces.
